parole.significato: Used to form genitive phrases, attached to the last word in a noun phrase.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish -s, from Old Norse -s, originally the genitive singular ending of a-stem nouns. Cognate with Danish -s. The frequent use of the suffix in written and modern colloquial Swedish is possibly the result of foreign influence, either Latin or Middle Low German.
From German aggressiv, French agressif.

parole.significato: an album, a book specially designed to keep photographs, stamps, or autographs
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin album or English album.

Either borrowed from German annoncieren (“advertise”) or French annoncer (“announce”). Derived from Old French anoncier, from Latin adnūntiāre. Ultimately affix of Latin ad- (“to”) + nūntiō (“announce, declare”). First attested in 1788.
Derived from French bandoulière, from Italian bandoliera or from Spanish bandolera.

parole.significato: freight, charter (hire a boat to use it for shipping)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German befrachten, or from Dutch bevrachten. Cognate of Danish befragte. By surface analysis, be- + frakta. First attested in 1723.

From Old Swedish bereþa, from Middle Low German bereden, from berede + -en or from be- + reden, equivalent to be- + reda. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål berede, Danish berede, Dutch bereiden, German bereiten.
From French bizarre, either from Basque bizar, "a beard" (the notion being that bearded Spanish soldiers made a strange impression on the French) or from Italian bizzarro.

parole.significato: to flash; to emit a flashing light
parole.testo: From either blixta or *blixra, from blixa, without close relatives in Scandinavian, but ultimately from Proto-Germanic *blīkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ-. Cognate of Dutch bliksemen, German blitzen.

parole.significato: boss, supervisor; someone who oversees work
parole.testo: Borrowed from English boss.

parole.significato: a small, controlled fire used for warmth
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brasō (“gleed, crackling coal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to seethe, boil, brew”), or from *bʰres- (“to crack, break, burst”).

parole.significato: a bird of the bulbul (Pycnonotidae) family
parole.testo: From Classical Persian بلبل (bulbul) or from Arabic بُلْبُل (bulbul).
Potentially to Latin bustum. Alternatively to older byste, buste, to Old Swedish bøste, from Old East Norse *bausti (“chest, breasts”) (cf. Old West Norse beysti).
Inherited from Old Swedish batsman, either from Middle Low German bōsman or Middle Dutch bōtsman. Equivalent to båt + -s- + man. Compare English boatsman, Dutch bootsman, German Bootsmann.
Borrowed from French dominance or from English dominance.

parole.significato: Inseparable verbal prefix that indicates an emphasizing meaning
parole.testo: From German er-, from Old High German ir-, and/or from Middle Low German er-, from Old Saxon ā-, both from Proto-Germanic *uz-.

From Old Swedish fīka f, fīkon n (plural), from Old Norse fíka, fíkja; formed using the fruit suffix + -on (neutral noun-forming suffix; used in the names of fruits and berries), an archaic variation from Old Norse -in. Originally either from Old English fīc or Vulgar Latin *fīca based on the -k- fo
From Middle Low German finne or from German Finne, perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *finnō. Related to English fin.

parole.significato: great, heartfelt joy; joy, delight, pleasure
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fryghþ, frygh, frøgdh, frøghdh, frøgd, frøghd, from Old Norse frygð, from Proto-Norse *ᚠᚱᛁᚷᚹᛁᚦᚢ (*friggwiþu), from Proto-Germanic *friwiþō; or possibly from *ᚠᚱᚢᚷᚹᛁᚦᚢ (*fruggwiþu), from Proto-Germanic *fruwiþō, both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frawaz. Cognate with Elfdalian fröj
Either derived from Middle Low German vorbloden or German verbluten. Equivalent to för- + blöda. Cognate of Danish forbløde. See also English forbleed.
Superficially equivalent to för- + färdig + -a, from either Middle Low German vorverdigen or German verfertigen. Cognate of Danish forfærdige.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorneme or from German vornehm. Cognate of Danish fornem. Originally with the sense "which can or should be taken before others".
From Old Swedish forthiǣnist or from för- + tjänst, from German Verdienst; a noun based on the verb förtjäna, German verdienen.

Either from German Gewehr, from Middle High German gewer, from Old High German giwerida or from Low German Gewehr. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål gevær, Danish gevær and Dutch geweer. Related to värja (“to defend, to protect”).

parole.significato: swerve, veer (quick turn to the side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gier (“yaw”), from gieren (“to yaw”), or from the Low German equivalent.

parole.significato: skin, complexion ((appearance of) skin on the face)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hý, from Proto-Germanic *hiwją, either from Proto-Indo-European *kew-, *ḱew- or from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-, or a merger of the two. Compare English hue.

parole.significato: A holiday, festival or similar festive occasion.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish höghtiþ with the same meaning (alternatively "wedding"), from Low German hochtid (“important religious or secular festivity”). Compare German Hochzeit (“wedding”).

Historically in the form em and im. The form em is from Old Swedish ēmber, from Old Norse eimr. The form im is either derived from em, or from Old Norse ím. From Proto-Germanic *aimaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ews-.

parole.significato: a card; a piece of stiff paper or plastic.
parole.testo: Probably from Danish kort (“a card”) or possibly from a not referenced Middle Low German word kort known in Low German, kort (“a card”). Cognate with Icelandic kort (“a card, a map”) and Faroese kort (“a card, a map”), both from Old Norse kort (“a map”), all based on a variant of the Latin words cha
From Spanish cochinilla, or from Ancient Greek κόκκινος (kókkinos, “red tint”), from κόκκος (kókkos), from Latin coccus (“berry or grain”).

parole.significato: a manger, a crib, a feeding trough for animals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krubba, from Old Norse krubba, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Cognate with German Krippe, English crib. Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German krübbe, kribbe, from Old Saxon kribbia, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ.

From Old Swedish kräkias, from Old Norse kræghe, from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn (“to crack, crackle, shriek”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to resound, cry hoarsely”). Cognate with Scots crak (“to crack”), West Frisian kreakje (“to crack”), Dutch kraken (“to crunch, creak, squeak”

From Old Swedish krønika, krønik, from Middle Low German kröneke ~ kroneke, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “relating to time”), derived from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Compare Danish and Norwegian krønike. It is not ruled out that the word was borrowed into Old Saxon ear

parole.significato: a certain small-diameter of timber, often from spruce or birch, usually about 3.1 m long, with lower quality requiremen…
parole.testo: From Old Norse kubbi, kobbi, to Proto-Germanic *kubb-. Probably related to kavel, kavle, to Proto-Germanic *kablaz (“round piece of wood; stick, rod”), to Proto-Indo-European *ǵebʰ- (“branch”) to a word family either referencing wood or shape (compare Swedish vedgubbe (“piece of firewood”), dynamitg

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: a lip (fleshy protrusion framing the mouth)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish læpper, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse *lep(p)r, derived from Proto-Germanic *lipn-, *lepn-, syncopated oblique forms of Proto-Germanic *lepô (“lip”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“lip”). Alternatively, perhaps from Old Norse *lepr, from Proto-Germanic *lepaz (“lip”)

mala + ström, from ström (“stream, streaming water”) and presumably from the verb mala (“to mill, to rotate like a mill stone, to swing around, to swirl”). Same as Old Danish malestrøm, Danish malstrøm, German Mahlstrom, English maelstrom, originally from Dutch maalstroom. Alternatively the first co

Old Swedish mölna, mylna (“mill”) (from Latin molīna), equivalent to mjöl + -na + -are (same construction as Old Norse Mjǫllnir (“the miller → the crusher”)). Alternatively directly from Late Latin molīnārius. Spelling influenced by mjöl (“flour, meal”), which shares a common Proto-Indo-European ety

Possibly an alteration of morgon (“morning”), or from Tavringer Romani mus, muss, musij, mossj, måssj (“man, person”), from Romani murś (“man”). Related to Sanskrit मनुष्य (manuṣya, “man”). Compare English mush.

From the greeting mors. Possibly an alteration of morgon (“morning”), or from Tavringer Romani mus, muss, musij, mossj, måssj (“man, person”), from Romani murś (“man”). Related to Sanskrit मनुष्य (manuṣya, “man”). Compare English mush.
From either German ratifizieren or French ratifier, from Medieval Latin ratificare, from Latin ratus (“fixed; certain”) + facere (“to make”). Compare origin to ratihabera.

Borrowed from Low German rēling, regeling or from Dutch reeling, regeling, from Middle Low German regel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably borrowed from Latin regula (“bar, rule”). Cognate of German Reling, English railing, Danish ræling.
From German Sekretariat or from French secrétariat, from Medieval Latin secretariatus, from Latin sēcrētārius (“secretary”).

parole.significato: a seal (a design usually representing some person or organization, an impression of that design on a document or other…
parole.testo: Attested since 1460–1461 as Old Swedish sighel, sägel (in the compounds sighla vax, sägelvax, referring to sealing wax), ultimately from Latin sigillum (see there for more). Compare Danish sigil, segl (including older forms such as segel, sigel), Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐌲𐌻𐌾𐍉 (sigljō), Middle Low German segel, segg

From Old Norse skemta, from either Proto-Germanic *skammatjaną or Proto-Germanic *skammitōną. Cognate with Faroese skemta, Norwegian Nynorsk skjemta, Icelandic skemmta, and Danish skæmte. Equivalent to skämt (“joke”) + -a.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smuk or from German Schmuck. Cognate of Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk smykke.

parole.significato: to flush (let water (or another liquid) flow over, usually in order clean, and usually at pressure), (when cleaning) to…
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German spölen, from Old Saxon spōlian, from Proto-West Germanic *spōlijan. Compare the older byform spöla. The back vowel could stem from Low German past forms with Rückumlaut. Alternatively it could be from Middle Dutch influence. Cognate with Danish spule, Norwegian Bokmål
stig + man. Borrowed from either Old Norse stigamaðr or Danish stimand.

parole.significato: to mutilate, to curtail, to shorten
parole.testo: Either borrowed from German stümpfen, related to German Stumpf (“stump”), or inherited from Old Swedish stympla, borrowed from Middle Low German stumpelen (from whence German verstümmeln).

parole.significato: stand; be in an upright position
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stā, possibly from an unattested eastern Old Norse stá, or via early Middle Low German stān. Both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stāną, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-. Or from earlier Swedish stånda, from Old Swedish staanda, standa, stonda, from Old Norse standa, from Proto-Germ
Either formed as an abstraction from the Swedish verb svälla, or borrowed from German Schwall (or Middle High German swal). Doublet of svullnad and svulst.
From either Middle Low German swans or German Schwanz.

Unknown. Possibly ultimately from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “flat of the foot, ankle, palm of the hand”) (probably through Latin tarsus by way of German Tarsus or French tarse; compare English tarsal). Perhaps the meaning extended from "flat surface of the foot or palm" to "paw of an animal." Co

parole.significato: a ground lot, a parcel (of land), that has had, currently has or in the future will have a house built on it. It especi…
parole.testo: From Old Norse toft, topt, tompt, from Proto-Germanic *tumþiz and/or from Proto-Germanic *tumftō, both from Proto-Indo-European *dm̥- (“to build”).
From Low German tuten, from Middle Low German tūten, either of imitative origin or derived from Proto-West Germanic *þeutan (“to howl”), itself probably imitative.

parole.significato: to think (think to oneself, have a thought (process) in one's head)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þænkia, from Middle Low German denken (“to perceive, think”), from Old Saxon thenkian. While nk attests to the Low German origin, the initial t must be due to influence by some inherited cognate. This is probably either tycka (“to have an opinion”) or Old Swedish þækkia (“to seem, t

parole.significato: a cake, a torte, a layered cake
parole.testo: From French tarte. The å sound [o:] might be due to either regular sound change, or interference from German Torte.
Borrowed from English undulate, or from Latin undulatus.
Likely from Middle Low German wankelmōdich or possibly from German wankelmütig.
From Old Swedish varmber, from Old Norse varmr, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”) or alternatively *wer- (“to burn”).

Possibly of Middle Low German origin (cf. Middle Low German adel), from Old Saxon ethiling, from Proto-West Germanic *aþuling, from Proto-Germanic *aþulingaz; alternatively from Old Norse ǫðlingr, ultimately from the same Proto-Germanic root.
